XDRTB - Cochlear Implant

By: Liz Fish | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

Summary:
Phumeza Tisile survived 3 gruelling years of Extreme Drug Resistant TB treatment but was stone deaf by the end of it - the drugs that saved her stole her hearing. 30% of patients treated for MDR TB experience this side-effect but it’s a choice between life and death. It starts with the loss of high frequency hearing which is often unnoticed and because it’s a rapid-onset loss of hearing, most state patients like Phumeza aren’t warned or given regular audio tests, so they wake up one morning stone deaf. But all that is about to change: on the 20th February, Phumeza will have a double cochlear implant thanks to a successful international fundraising campaign.

Further information:
Phumeza is extremely fortunate that she is a good candidate for cochlear implants, and is getting both at the same time, so her chances of recovering her hearing are good. But it is a slow and frustrating process, and her brain will have to learn how to interpret electronic sounds as opposed to acoustic sound, which can take anything up to six months. When the implants are “switched on” it will be cacophony of noise inside her head.
Nurse Jolene Samuels contracted MDR TB at work and went totally deaf despite knowing the dangers of the treatment. The drugs not only made her deaf but damaged the nerves in her feet and she is now partially crippled and no longer able to work. This mother of two wasn’t able to hear the first words her newborn uttered. She lost her marriage, her friends and her income. Jolene was lucky enough to be able to claim occupational disease benefits and so the state covered the costs. Cochlear implants are extremely expensive and medical aids only partially cover the costs. Often patients can only afford one implant, which is extremely challenging because they can’t work out where sounds are coming from.
Medical practitioners are 80% more at risk of contracted MDR and XDR TB than the average person. Dr Dalene von Delft was one of those casualties, when she contracted MDR TB, she was well-informed about the side-effects of the treatment and had regular audiograms. To her horror, she discovered she was rapidly losing her high frequency hearing which continued even after she stopped the treatment. Miraculously she managed to get onto a compassionate trial of Bedaquiline, the new TB drug, and today she is only partially deaf. Dr von Delft says she has never heard of anybody successfully suing a drug company for hearing loss and the only drugs available to treat drug resistant TB are extremely old and contain aminoglycosides which can cause hearing loss.
Since my last insert on MDR and XDR TB, Bedaquiline has become available in South Africa and is undergoing its last phase of medical trials. However, it is only available for 3000 of the 15000 known patients because the drug is so expensive - 4000 of these patients are likely to be left permanently deaf.
The insert will be shot over several months, starting with Phumeza’s cochlear implant operation on the 20th February. The next shoot will be when they first switch the implants on a few weeks later, and then again several months later. Dr Van Delft has been instrumental in assisting Phumeza with the fund-raising campaign and is now working for an NGO called TB Proof which is raising awareness around TB treatment. Jolene Samuels will speak about her experiences learning to hear with implants, and will be supporting Phumeza on the difficult and often frustrating journey of trying to hear again.
Dr Gill Kerr is Phumeza’s audiologist at Tygerberg hospital. She says there is an increasing number of MDR TB patients being referred to her and many patients are not suitable candidates or cannot afford implants and will spend the rest of their lives in silence. Dr Kerr has been working with Phumeza for months and is confident she will next year be able to return to her studies which were so brutally interrupted by TB four years ago.


Extra Budget Items:
The filming will have to happen over several months and will require more shoot days and travelling than the normal insert.

Viewing Notes:
We watched it again – new notes

• Make intro more dramatic – she lost her hearing 5 years ago in a cruel twist of fate explain why she is unique
• Put sub titles on Phumeza throughout please except at the end when we go back to her after 3 ½ months where she speaks more clearly
• When was the op? When is three and a half months later? When is TB day?
• Put the date in on all the CB archive stuff upfront
• Explain that the injectible drug causes deafness as KNOWN side-effect and people take it knowing that risk
• Tell us in script that Extremely drug resistant TB is XDR-TB in the first voice over
• You say she had XDR TB and that Dalene had MDR TB – it sounds like they had the same thing. Please clarify they are both forms of TB but the one is less severe – clarify they are different
• Black and white/tone down somehow the surgery shots showing the implant go in and in the promos – viewers wont be able to handle them.
• Yabo – this should be Haibo shouldn’t it? Please double check that i am not sure of the spelling
• “how is this god” – what does that mean is it a question?
• Take out the reference to CB not having sub titles
• Tweak the mom’s one slightly to say “God is great”
• Please can you put in visuals of her with both implants
• Cut to 10 mins exactly or under 10 – you can cut out around the world TB day stuff.
• Dalene – you can leave her as is structure wise.

Not sure of the durations of these and which is which in terms of 15 / ten second and which is the tues 10 second promo :
1. Promo 1 – its odd when she asks how she is and she says right. Rather show them crying and the emotion and cut those sound ups out.
2. Promo 2: doesn’t tell us this is a story of hope and healing deafness brought on by TB. Viewers wont tune in to watch a TB story only. Write a new one and make it more about the miracle of the story – eg drugs to treat XDR-TB made her go deaf. A doctor that experienced the same got involved and now she’s hearing again for the fisrt time
3. Promo 3: nice but subtitle her
4. Promo 4: no - same comment as promo 2. Please re-write - thanks

Press Release:


Phumeza’s Miracle
Phumeza Tisile survived three gruelling years of Extreme Drug Resistant TB. But overcoming this illness came at a very high price. The drugs also destroyed her hearing. Thirty percent of patients treated for Multi Drug Resistant TB experience this horrific side-effect. But refusing treatment means choosing death. Now, Carte Blanche joins this brave young woman as a double cochlear implant, paid for through an international fundraising campaign, sees her hear her mother’s voice again for the first time.


Script:


Script: Five years ago Phumeza Tsilie went completely deaf overnight. She suffered one of the worst side effects from the injectable drug used to treat Multiple drug resistant TB. Since then she has struggled to communicate as she is unable to use sign language and only lip reads Xhosa

Phumeza : One morning I wake up and I turned the TV on and I could not hear and I thought the volume must be down I turned the volume up and still not I thought there was something in my ear. After I got deaf there was no counseling for me I had to deal with that on my own.

Script: Having survived a 3 year battle against Extremely Drug Resistant TB and witnessing many others dying around her, Phumeza began campaigning for better, safer drugs. This is how she met Dr Dalene von Delft, fellow Multiple Drug Resistant TB survivor and activist who had suffered partial hearing loss from the injectable drug. When she heard Phumeza’s story she felt an immediate connection

Dalene “I first met Phumeza actually online when she was blogging and I was still a TB patient and I felt very isolated and alone . I think the first time I met her was like meeting a friend except I saw the sadness in her eyes because she was shut out from the world

Script: There was one hope for Phumeza’s hearing to be restored – a cochlear implant. So, Phumeza and Dalene started a fund raising campaign. Phumeza’s activist profile saw the money coming in from around the globe and they raised half a million rand, enough for a double cochlear implant

Dalene “I can’t believe that we managed to do. I am super excited for Phumeza, really so so elated,so happy

Phumeza “Well I am a bit nervous but at the same time excited because I have waited a long time for this to happen, now finally it is happening

Script: In February this year a team of specialists led by Dr Gary Kroukamp undertook the life changing surgery.

Upsound in theatre “ My assistant today is Derek Wagenveld who did the first cochlear implant in South Africa in 1986 and I was still in High School at the time so its quite reassuring to have him here in case anything funny happens.

Script: It was an intricate 4 hour operation with some tense moments

Dr Kroukamp “We had to drill about a 2 mm slot between the facial nerve and one of its branches so we have to be very very careful in that situation because if you damage that facial nerve the person will end up with weakness on one side of their face and the other really tricky moment really because of the high cost of the implant itself if you do it incorrectly you may damage the electrode array and then have to discard it and we are talking R250 000 worth, piece of equipment

Script: The inner ear has 3000 hairs which pick up acoustic signals and send them to the brain. The cochlear implant has only has 22 receptors which transmit digital signals so Audiologist Gill Kerr will work with Phumeza for the next year helping her brain relearn the new sound.

Gill “The cochlear implant picks up sound through a microphone and encodes it into a digital signal it sends it to the coil that Phumeza wears on the side of her head , a transmitting coil and by radio frequencies it sends those signals to the implant receiver which is just underneath the skin.

Script: The implant receiver transmits signals via 22 Platinum wires in the cochlear implant bypassing the damaged inner ear hair cells

Link: Well it’s been four weeks since the operation, and today is Phumeza’s big day, after 5 years of complete silence her implants are about to be switched on. It’s also a day of mixed emotions because for some people the results can be disappointing

Gill “When I am talking to you is there something happening?
Phumeza “ Yip “

Gill “ Oh what is happening?”
Phumeza “No I am listening to you, I am calm, you are sounding like a robot
Gill “I am sounding like a robot . That is a good start

Mom “ Phumeza how are you?”
Phumeza “Right.
Mom “Hayibo Are you alright can you hear me”
Phumeza “Well”
Mom “I am so happy to hear you – how great is God?

Script: Phumeza had not heard her mother’s voice for 5 years, she was overwhelmed

Phumeza “Let’s hear Dalene. “
Dalene “I can’t talk I am crying”

UPSOUND Gill “So in the beginning with a cochlear implant the sound is different to how you used to hear before you lost your hearing so your brain is going to start getting used to a new kind of sound “

Phumeza “I don’t sound like you, you sound like a cartoon from Spongebob

Gill “Its very hard for a patient to predict how they will respond on the day of switch on and very natural to feel anxious and nervous before the time you don’t know what is going to happen

John “Phumeza today has been a very big day for you It’s been an amazing day”

Phumeza “Can you repeat that? –

John” It’s been an incredible day for you”

Phumeza” Yes it’s been amazing I will put it in my diary in bold letters”

John “Well Dalene a wonderful day for Phumeza but how are you feeling right now?”

Dalene “ Well today I feel very emotional actually it’s been quite a long journey not only for Phumeza but for me walking with her, a lot of struggles that we had along the way. We tried to keep our expectations low and but we were so surprised at the amazing results. It’s probably one of the best moments of my life

Script: We came back after the weekend to see how Phumeza was coping

Phumeza “A miracle because I didn’t think I would hear again especially when they told me the price of the implants I was oh oh I don’t think I will make it but then I did and I am hearing again. I can’t wait to hear music and be on the telephone having a normal conversation with people

John “Was the quietness difficult for you?

Phumeza “Ahhh it was depressing but I was like my own psychologist, so I read many books to get my mind off things

Script: One third of Multiple Drug Resistant TB patients suffer hearing loss, which can continue to deteriorate even after going off the injection. Dalene‘s monthly hearing test in 2010 showed she was losing her hear high frequency hearing. Her doctor gave her a stark choice

Dalene “He said it’s either deaf or you’re dead. I realized I wouldn’t be able to listen over the phone, have a dinner conversation .If am deaf I can’t speak to patients I can’t use my stethoscope so it was ending my career

Script: She went off the injection and got onto a new drug called Bedaqiline

Dalene “Bedaquiline is good but it is not enough. Currently there are a lot of trials going on to trying to get what we call a regimen for TB of at least 3 but preferably 4 effective drugs. And luckily there is some hope on the horizon

Link: Medical staff are more at risk of contracting TB than the general population and one third of those who get the disease end up losing their lives. Alarmingly because people are often admitted hospital without being properly diagnosed medical professionals are 6 times more likely to get multi and extreme drug resistant TB.

Link “Dalene contracted Multi Drug resistant TB while working as a doctor at Tygerberg Hospital. After 18 months of treatment she was finally cured but felt had to leave the public health system rather than risk reinfection. At the moment she is working as an activist campaigning to educate other health workers to protect themselves

Dalene “I realized that a lot of my colleagues got ill from TB some even died from drug resistant TB , and we are all healthy young professionals and it is something nobody talks about.

UPsound Dalene “But my message to you is that anyone can get TB, that is why it is everyone’s problem, and everyone should protect themselves, and because you are medical students you are already at risk of contracting Tuberculosis

Script: Despite still battling to distinguish sounds four days after the switch on, Phumeza joined in the discussion undaunted

Upsound Phumeza: Many are left deaf, I was lucky enough to get a cochlear implant as you know TB is the diseases of the poor, right? So not everybody can afford the implants for me to afford it took some sweat, right? So tomorrow as you all know is World TB day, right, so it will be great if you can all wear your masks and put your selfies on the Unmask Stigma Campaign

Link ( June 2015 in Caption top right) Well it’s been three and half months since Phumeza had her Cochlear implants switched on. We saw how dramatically her life changed in those first few days so it will be interesting to see how she is doing now. We are one the way to her house in Khayelitsha where we are going to sit down and have a chat

Phumeza “Well now things have changed drastically because people no longer sound like robots they sound like people and the background sounds no longer disturb me like it did the first day before I didn’t want to socialize because it was awkward for me, now things have changed I go out make phone calls watch TV, the fun stuff I am back to life again. But then she said it will be much better let’s say at the end of the year everything will be normal so I just have to wait and see

Upsound Gill “So these are some sentences that I am going to say and I want you to try and repeat what you think I said. It’s a new book
Phumeza “It’s a new book”

Gill “She is a very motivated person there are few of my patients that have had to go into as many different listening situations that Phumeza has had in the last few months in terms of her TB activism and the other work that she is doing as well and she doesn’t let her hearing stand in the way she just carries on and tries her best in each situation. And I think that is part of what makes her so successful

John’ Dalene seems to have invested herself emotionally with you is there something you would you like to say to her?

Phumeza “Hmm emotional part. I mean she is like an angel if I may say so myself”

John: “You have dealt with this extraordinary challenge Phumeza, so incredibly well, what do you think that say about the person you are

Phumeza “Perhaps I have that positive vibes on me like I don’t want to focus on the negative side of things

Script: Their fight to survive Multiple and extremely resistant TB left Phumeza and Dalene with one message: TB is not a death sentence if you take the drugs. They will continue to fight for better safer drugs

Script: It was an intricate 4 hour operation with some tense moments Dr Kroukamp “We had to drill about a 2 mm slot between the facial nerve and one of its branches so we have to be very very careful in that situation because if you damage that facial nerve the person will end up with weakness on one side of their face and the other really tricky moment really because of the high cost of the implant itself if you do it incorrectly you may damage the electrode array and then have to discard it and we are talking R250 000 worth, piece of equipment Script: The inner ear has 3000 hairs which pick up acoustic signals and send them to the brain. The cochlear implant has only has 22 receptors which transmit digital signals so Audiologist Gill Kerr will work with Phumeza for the next year helping her brain relearn the new sound. Gill “The cochlear implant picks up sound through a microphone and encodes it into a digital signal it sends it to the coil that Phumeza wears on the side of her head , a transmitting coil and by radio frequencies it sends those signals to the implant receiver which is just underneath the skin. Script: The implant receiver transmits signals via 22 Platinum wires in the cochlear implant bypassing the damaged inner ear hair cells Link: Well it’s been four weeks since the operation, and today is Phumeza’s big day, after 5 years of complete silence her implants are about to be switched on. It’s also a day of mixed emotions because for some people the results can be disappointing Gill “When I am talking to you is there something happening? Phumeza “ Yip “ Gill “ Oh what is happening?” Phumeza “No I am listening to you, I am calm, you are sounding like a robot Gill “I am sounding like a robot . That is a good start Mom “ Phumeza how are you?” Phumeza “Right. Mom “Hayibo Are you alright can you hear me” Phumeza “Well” Mom “I am so happy to hear you – how great is God? Script: Phumeza had not heard her mother’s voice for 5 years, she was overwhelmed Phumeza “Let’s hear Dalene. “ Dalene “I can’t talk I am crying” UPSOUND Gill “So in the beginning with a cochlear implant the sound is different to how you used to hear before you lost your hearing so your brain is going to start getting used to a new kind of sound “ Phumeza “I don’t sound like you, you sound like a cartoon from Spongebob Gill “Its very hard for a patient to predict how they will respond on the day of switch on and very natural to feel anxious and nervous before the time you don’t know what is going to happen John “Phumeza today has been a very big day for you It’s been an amazing day” Phumeza “Can you repeat that? – John” It’s been an incredible day for you” Phumeza” Yes it’s been amazing I will put it in my diary in bold letters” John “Well Dalene a wonderful day for Phumeza but how are you feeling right now?” Dalene “ Well today I feel very emotional actually it’s been quite a long journey not only for Phumeza but for me walking with her, a lot of struggles that we had along the way. We tried to keep our expectations low and but we were so surprised at the amazing results. It’s probably one of the best moments of my life Script: We came back after the weekend to see how Phumeza was coping Phumeza “A miracle because I didn’t think I would hear again especially when they told me the price of the implants I was oh oh I don’t think I will make it but then I did and I am hearing again. I can’t wait to hear music and be on the telephone having a normal conversation with people John “Was the quietness difficult for you? Phumeza “Ahhh it was depressing but I was like my own psychologist, so I read many books to get my mind off things Script: One third of Multiple Drug Resistant TB patients suffer hearing loss, which can continue to deteriorate even after going off the injection. Dalene‘s monthly hearing test in 2010 showed she was losing her hear high frequency hearing. Her doctor gave her a stark choice Dalene “He said it’s either deaf or you’re dead. I realized I wouldn’t be able to listen over the phone, have a dinner conversation .If am deaf I can’t speak to patients I can’t use my stethoscope so it was ending my career Script: She went off the injection and got onto a new drug called Bedaqiline Dalene “Bedaquiline is good but it is not enough. Currently there are a lot of trials going on to trying to get what we call a regimen for TB of at least 3 but preferably 4 effective drugs. And luckily there is some hope on the horizon Link: Medical staff are more at risk of contracting TB than the general population and one third of those who get the disease end up losing their lives. Alarmingly because people are often admitted hospital without being properly diagnosed medical professionals are 6 times more likely to get multi and extreme drug resistant TB. Link “Dalene contracted Multi Drug resistant TB while working as a doctor at Tygerberg Hospital. After 18 months of treatment she was finally cured but felt had to leave the public health system rather than risk reinfection. At the moment she is working as an activist campaigning to educate other health workers to protect themselves Dalene “I realized that a lot of my colleagues got ill from TB some even died from drug resistant TB , and we are all healthy young professionals and it is something nobody talks about. UPsound Dalene “But my message to you is that anyone can get TB, that is why it is everyone’s problem, and everyone should protect themselves, and because you are medical students you are already at risk of contracting Tuberculosis Script: Despite still battling to distinguish sounds four days after the switch on, Phumeza joined in the discussion undaunted Upsound Phumeza: Many are left deaf, I was lucky enough to get a cochlear implant as you know TB is the diseases of the poor, right? So not everybody can afford the implants for me to afford it took some sweat, right? So tomorrow as you all know is World TB day, right, so it will be great if you can all wear your masks and put your selfies on the Unmask Stigma Campaign Link ( June 2015 in Caption top right) Well it’s been three and half months since Phumeza had her Cochlear implants switched on. We saw how dramatically her life changed in those first few days so it will be interesting to see how she is doing now. We are one the way to her house in Khayelitsha where we are going to sit down and have a chat Phumeza “Well now things have changed drastically because people no longer sound like robots they sound like people and the background sounds no longer disturb me like it did the first day before I didn’t want to socialize because it was awkward for me, now things have changed I go out make phone calls watch TV, the fun stuff I am back to life again. But then she said it will be much better let’s say at the end of the year everything will be normal so I just have to wait and see Upsound Gill “So these are some sentences that I am going to say and I want you to try and repeat what you think I said. It’s a new book Phumeza “It’s a new book” Gill “She is a very motivated person there are few of my patients that have had to go into as many different listening situations that Phumeza has had in the last few months in terms of her TB activism and the other work that she is doing as well and she doesn’t let her hearing stand in the way she just carries on and tries her best in each situation. And I think that is part of what makes her so successful John’ Dalene seems to have invested herself emotionally with you is there something you would you like to say to her? Phumeza “Hmm emotional part. I mean she is like an angel if I may say so myself” John: “You have dealt with this extraordinary challenge Phumeza, so incredibly well, what do you think that say about the person you are Phumeza “Perhaps I have that positive vibes on me like I don’t want to focus on the negative side of things Script: Their fight to survive Multiple and extremely resistant TB left Phumeza and Dalene with one message: TB is not a death sentence if you take the drugs. They will continue to fight for better safer drugs Invoicing Back references from Insert ID in Invoice: Title Author Last Updated Invoice for XDRTB - Cochlear Implant (4508 ) lizfish@iafrica.com 02 July 2015

metadata.Summary: Phumeza Tisile survived 3 gruelling years of Extreme Drug Resistant TB treatment but was stone deaf by the end of it - the drugs that saved her stole her hearing. 30% of patients treated for MDR TB experience this side-effect but it’s a choice between life and death. It starts with the loss of high frequency hearing which is often unnoticed and because it’s a rapid-onset loss of hearing, most state patients like Phumeza aren’t warned or given regular audio tests, so they wake up one morning stone deaf. But all that is about to change: on the 20th February, Phumeza will have a double cochlear implant thanks to a successful international fundraising campaign.
metadata.Further information: Phumeza is extremely fortunate that she is a good candidate for cochlear implants, and is getting both at the same time, so her chances of recovering her hearing are good. But it is a slow and frustrating process, and her brain will have to learn how to interpret electronic sounds as opposed to acoustic sound, which can take anything up to six months. When the implants are “switched on” it will be cacophony of noise inside her head. Nurse Jolene Samuels contracted MDR TB at work and went totally deaf despite knowing the dangers of the treatment. The drugs not only made her deaf but damaged the nerves in her feet and she is now partially crippled and no longer able to work. This mother of two wasn’t able to hear the first words her newborn uttered. She lost her marriage, her friends and her income. Jolene was lucky enough to be able to claim occupational disease benefits and so the state covered the costs. Cochlear implants are extremely expensive and medical aids only partially cover the costs. Often patients can only afford one implant, which is extremely challenging because they can’t work out where sounds are coming from. Medical practitioners are 80% more at risk of contracted MDR and XDR TB than the average person. Dr Dalene von Delft was one of those casualties, when she contracted MDR TB, she was well-informed about the side-effects of the treatment and had regular audiograms. To her horror, she discovered she was rapidly losing her high frequency hearing which continued even after she stopped the treatment. Miraculously she managed to get onto a compassionate trial of Bedaquiline, the new TB drug, and today she is only partially deaf. Dr von Delft says she has never heard of anybody successfully suing a drug company for hearing loss and the only drugs available to treat drug resistant TB are extremely old and contain aminoglycosides which can cause hearing loss. Since my last insert on MDR and XDR TB, Bedaquiline has become available in South Africa and is undergoing its last phase of medical trials. However, it is only available for 3000 of the 15000 known patients because the drug is so expensive - 4000 of these patients are likely to be left permanently deaf. The insert will be shot over several months, starting with Phumeza’s cochlear implant operation on the 20th February. The next shoot will be when they first switch the implants on a few weeks later, and then again several months later. Dr Van Delft has been instrumental in assisting Phumeza with the fund-raising campaign and is now working for an NGO called TB Proof which is raising awareness around TB treatment. Jolene Samuels will speak about her experiences learning to hear with implants, and will be supporting Phumeza on the difficult and often frustrating journey of trying to hear again. Dr Gill Kerr is Phumeza’s audiologist at Tygerberg hospital. She says there is an increasing number of MDR TB patients being referred to her and many patients are not suitable candidates or cannot afford implants and will spend the rest of their lives in silence. Dr Kerr has been working with Phumeza for months and is confident she will next year be able to return to her studies which were so brutally interrupted by TB four years ago.
